changes.name: collaboration-framework
changes.before: Composite framework/operational skill for working with an LLM to engineering standards — character, craft, and the disciplines holding the quality floor. Grounded in the collaboration-framework posture guide set, engineering methodology, and operational guidance for ledger discipline, project management, code audit, testing, subagent delegation, contribution style, and scientific-methods routing. Use when: sustained, high-stakes sessions — deep study, research, expert systems design, or production programming; establishing the peer frame; planning or closing a project, arc, or slice (MUST read the project-management guides README first); Expedited Mode; running the 9-point SDLC or a ledgered slice; commissioning an audit; hardening tests; delegating lookup work; drafting contribution tickets; or recognizing when controlled inquiry/regression comparison should load scientific-methods. Does NOT load domain/tooling skills under sibling knowledge roots — loaded separately, per-domain.
changes.after: LLM collaboration for sustained research and engineering; planning/closing projects, arcs or slices; Expedited Mode; ledgered SDLC, audits, testing, delegation, contribution tickets and experiments. Read project-management guides before planning/closure. Load domain skills separately.
changes.rationale: Front-loads the work and retains operational triggers, planning prerequisite, and separate domain loading. Provenance and detailed posture remain in the body. Review whether peer-frame terminology warrants replacing another phrase.

changes.name: cobalt-guidelines
changes.before: Comprehensive guidelines for building, extending, and deploying static sites with Cobalt — a Rust-native static site generator powered by Liquid templates — grounded in the official Cobalt documentation, the `cobalt-org/cobalt.rs` source, the `cobalt-config` schema, and the Rust `liquid` crate family (`liquid`, `liquid-core`, `liquid-lib`, `liquid-derive`). Use when: installing Cobalt, scaffolding a new site, authoring pages or posts, designing layouts and includes, writing Liquid templates (`{{ }}` output, `{% %}` logic, filters, tags, control flow), configuring `_cobalt.yml`, setting up permalinks, pagination, RSS, syntax highlighting, Sass/SCSS, data files, draft/publish workflow, debugging builds with `cobalt debug`, deploying to GitHub Pages / GitLab CI / self-hosting, or extending Cobalt programmatically in Rust via `cobalt::Config`, `liquid::ParserBuilder`, `Template`, `Object`/`Value`, and the `ObjectView`/`ValueView` traits.
changes.after: Build, configure, debug, extend, or deploy Cobalt static sites. Use for pages/posts, Liquid templates, layouts/includes, _cobalt.yml, permalinks, pagination, RSS, Sass, data, publishing, CI deployment, or Rust extensions using cobalt and liquid crates.
changes.rationale: Keeps Cobalt, Liquid, configuration, authoring, deployment, and Rust extension triggers; removes the source bibliography and individual API symbols. Requests naming only low-level Liquid traits need routing review.

changes.name: erlang-guidelines
changes.before: Comprehensive Erlang/OTP best practices, idioms, and anti-patterns grounded in the Erlang Programming Rules and Conventions, the OTP Design Principles, the Erlang Reference Manual and Efficiency Guide, Inaka's coding guidelines, "Erlang in Anger", "Learn You Some Erlang", and the EDoc user's guide. Use when: writing new Erlang code, refactoring existing Erlang, reviewing Erlang for issues, designing module APIs and return conventions, modelling data with records/maps/binaries and dialyzer typespecs, designing processes and message protocols, writing OTP behaviours, building supervision trees and applications/releases, applying let-it-crash fault tolerance, profiling and tuning on the BEAM, diagnosing live systems, writing eunit/common_test/PropEr tests, documenting with EDoc and OTP-27 -doc attributes, running distributed Erlang, or wiring the rebar3 + dialyzer + xref + elvis + erlfmt toolchain.
changes.after: Write, review, refactor, test, or diagnose Erlang/OTP systems. Use for APIs, typespecs, processes/messages, OTP behaviours, supervision, fault tolerance, releases, distributed Erlang, BEAM performance, EUnit/Common Test/PropEr, EDoc, or rebar3/dialyzer/xref/elvis/erlfmt tooling.
changes.rationale: Retains development, runtime diagnosis, OTP design, distribution, testing, documentation, and toolchain triggers. Removes bibliographic detail and examples of data representations.

changes.name: rust-guidelines
changes.before: Comprehensive Rust best practices, idioms, and anti-patterns grounded in the Rust Reference, the Rustonomicon, the Rust API Guidelines, the Rust Performance Book, the Asynchronous Programming Book, the Rustdoc Book, the Edition Guide, the Cargo Book, the tokio tutorial, and a corpus of AI-audited anti-patterns. Use when: writing new Rust code, refactoring existing Rust, reviewing Rust for issues, debugging ownership/lifetime errors, designing public APIs, handling errors with `Result`/`?`/`thiserror`/`anyhow`, wiring concurrency (`Send`/`Sync`, threads, channels, `async`/`await`, `Pin`, `Tokio`), writing declarative or procedural macros, working with `unsafe` and FFI boundaries, organising crates and workspaces, writing rustdoc, choosing or migrating a Rust edition, instrumenting code with `tracing`/`log`/metrics, building CLI tools with `clap`, or managing Cargo projects end-to-end.
changes.after: Write, review, refactor, or debug Rust. Use for ownership/lifetimes, public APIs, errors, async/Tokio and concurrency, macros, unsafe/FFI, crates/workspaces, rustdoc, edition migration, tracing/metrics, clap CLIs, and Cargo workflows.
changes.rationale: Keeps the distinct Rust task families and major ecosystem triggers. Removes source-book names and redundant API enumerations; specific Result, Pin, and Send/Sync requests should be checked in routing evaluation.

changes.name: cpp-guidelines
changes.before: Comprehensive C++ best practices, idioms, and anti-patterns grounded in the ISO C++ Core Guidelines by Bjarne Stroustrup, Herb Sutter, and contributors. Use when: writing new C++ code, refactoring existing C++ code, reviewing C++ for correctness or style issues, designing APIs and ownership boundaries, applying RAII/resource management, choosing parameter and return conventions, working with classes/value types/templates/concepts, handling exceptions and noexcept, diagnosing lifetime/null/dangling-pointer hazards, using the standard library, modernizing C-style or legacy C++, wiring CMake/tooling, or triaging generated C++ for safety, concurrency, performance, and idiom drift.
changes.after: Write, review, refactor, or modernize C++ using the Core Guidelines. Use for API/ownership design, RAII, lifetimes, classes, templates/concepts, exceptions/noexcept, the standard library, concurrency, performance, CMake, or generated-code review.
changes.rationale: Preserves modern C++ development, ownership, language facilities, tooling, and generated-code review. Consolidates pointer hazards into lifetimes and drops author provenance.

changes.name: go-guidelines
changes.before: Comprehensive Go best practices, idioms, and anti-patterns grounded in the Uber Go Style Guide, the Google Go Style Guide (Style Guide, Decisions, Best Practices), Effective Go, and the official Go spec. Use when: writing new Go code, refactoring existing Go, reviewing Go for issues, designing package APIs, handling errors with `errors.Is`/`%w`, propagating `context.Context`, wiring concurrency (channels, goroutines, `sync`), writing table-driven tests with `testing`, profiling with `testing.B` and `pprof`, organizing modules and packages, writing `godoc`-visible doc comments, or building Gio desktop UIs.
changes.after: Write, review, refactor, test, or profile Go. Use for package APIs, error wrapping, context propagation, goroutines/channels/sync, table-driven tests, benchmarks/pprof, modules, godoc, and Gio desktop UIs, following Go idioms and style guidance.
changes.rationale: Retains Go-specific task coverage, including the less-obvious Gio UI trigger. Replaces the bibliography and API spellings with their task meanings.

changes.name: javascript-deno-guidelines
changes.before: JavaScript and Deno best practices, idioms, and anti-patterns for this project. Use when: writing new JS code, refactoring existing JS, reviewing JS for issues, designing module APIs, handling errors, writing Deno tests, configuring deno.json tasks, preparing modules for JSR publishing, converting Node-style or TypeScript-style code to project idioms, doing code quality audits, performance reviews, improving documentation, making dependency decisions, configuring Biome lint/format, enforcing the no-Node boundary, or answering JS design questions.
changes.after: Write, review, refactor, or design JavaScript/Deno code using project idioms. Use for APIs, errors, Deno tests/tasks, JSR publishing, Node/TypeScript migration, performance, documentation, dependencies, or Biome configuration. Enforce the project's no-Node boundary.
changes.rationale: Keeps Deno, JSR, migration, design, quality review, and Biome triggers while explicitly preserving the project no-Node boundary.

changes.name: scientific-methods
changes.before: Method skill for practical scientific inquiry, experiment planning, controlled comparisons, regression tests, evaluation rubrics, evidence capture, and threats-to-validity analysis. Use when a conversation asks to test whether a change helped, compare versions or prompts, design an A/B trial, make an investigation more rigorous, define operational measures, or turn a fuzzy question into an inspectable protocol. Not for ordinary implementation unless the work needs explicit experimental design.
changes.after: Design scientific inquiries, controlled comparisons, A/B trials, and regression evaluations. Use to test whether a change helped, compare versions/prompts, define measures/rubrics, capture evidence, or assess validity. Not for ordinary implementation without explicit experimental design.
changes.rationale: Keeps inquiry design, comparison, measurement, evidence, validity, and the exclusion for ordinary implementation. Removes repeated descriptions of making an inquiry inspectable.

changes.name: visual-design-system
changes.before: Visual design principles, colour, typography, layout, and spatial composition for Cowboys & Beans projects. Use when: designing web pages or components, choosing colours, setting up type scales, composing layouts, writing CSS, building design tokens, creating fluid responsive designs, reviewing visual quality, breaking out of template patterns, designing navigation/wayfinding, theming across multiple sites, or answering any visual design question.
changes.after: Design or review visuals for Cowboys & Beans web pages and components. Use for colour, typography, layout, CSS, design tokens, responsive composition, navigation/wayfinding, cross-site theming, or improving visual quality beyond template patterns.
changes.rationale: Preserves the project identity and major visual-design triggers. Consolidates the catchall into design/review and omits repeated examples of choosing colours and type scales.

changes.name: biome-linter
changes.before: JavaScript/TypeScript/JSX/CSS linting guidance based on Biome's 394 lint rules. Use when writing, reviewing, or refactoring JS/TS/JSX/CSS code to catch bugs, enforce style consistency, improve accessibility, avoid performance pitfalls, and prevent security vulnerabilities. Covers correctness, suspicious patterns, style, complexity, a11y, performance, and security categories.
changes.after: Apply Biome lint guidance when writing, reviewing, or refactoring JavaScript, TypeScript, JSX, or CSS. Use for correctness, suspicious patterns, style, complexity, accessibility, performance, and security issues.
changes.rationale: Retains language scope and all rule categories while removing the brittle rule count and duplicated claims about benefits.

changes.name: tailwindcss
changes.before: Tailwind CSS v4 utility-first styling with CSS-native configuration. Use when styling with Tailwind utility classes, configuring themes via @theme, building responsive/dark-mode layouts, creating custom utilities or variants, or working with container queries. Covers the complete v4 API including @theme, @utility, @custom-variant, @variant, @source, and all utility classes.
changes.after: Style interfaces with Tailwind CSS v4. Use for utility classes, CSS-native configuration, @theme, responsive/dark-mode layouts, container queries, custom utilities/variants, and @source registration.
changes.rationale: Keeps the v4 boundary, configuration, layout, extension, and source-discovery triggers. Consolidates directive spellings and drops the exhaustive API claim.

changes.name: biome-js-linter
changes.before: Pure JavaScript/ECMAScript linting guidance based on Biome's lint rules, filtered to language-level concerns only. No React, Node.js, JSX, CSS, or framework-specific rules. Use when writing, reviewing, or refactoring vanilla JavaScript to catch bugs, avoid pitfalls, enforce idiomatic style, simplify code, and prevent performance or security issues.
changes.after: Apply Biome's language-level lint guidance when writing, reviewing, or refactoring vanilla JavaScript/ECMAScript. Covers bugs, idioms, complexity, performance, and security. Excludes React, Node.js, JSX, CSS, and framework-specific rules.
changes.rationale: Keeps language-only scope and every explicit exclusion, distinguishing this skill from the broader Biome web linter.

changes.name: deno-js-linter
changes.before: Pure JavaScript/ECMAScript linting guidance based on Deno's lint rules, filtered to language-level concerns only. No React, JSX, Fresh, Deno-specific, Node.js-specific, or TypeScript type-system rules. Use when writing, reviewing, or refactoring vanilla JavaScript to catch bugs, avoid pitfalls, and enforce idiomatic style.
changes.after: Apply Deno's language-level lint guidance when writing, reviewing, or refactoring vanilla JavaScript/ECMAScript. Excludes React, JSX, Fresh, Deno/Node runtime rules, and TypeScript type-system rules.
changes.rationale: Preserves the pure-JavaScript task and each exclusion; clarifies that Deno supplies the rules without making runtime-specific rules part of this skill.
